Zhang et al. 2025, Cleaner Energy Systems 12, 100223, Table 1 / supplementary Table S1: Material Production, Construction and Operation at the printed amounts, plus the refrigerant top-up emitted as a leak (ADDED). Transportation (delivery to site), Disposal and Recycling (end-of-life, with their credits) are outside the boundary. Functional unit is the whole facility over its 25-year operating life, not a per-kWh or per-m^2 unit.
bw:373047499921895424.source:
Data centre facility — Zhang et al. 2025, Virginia hyperscale.

Source and scope
Materials-production + operation inventory for a representative hyperscale
data centre (10,000 m² white space, Virginia US, SERC grid, PUE 1.4 baseline,
25-year operating life), from Zhang, M., Carbajales-Dale, M., Ma, X., Guo, L.,
Fan, C. (2025). "Cleaner grid or smarter cooling? Environmental impact
trade-offs of a data center using the life cycle assessment method." *Cleaner
Energy Systems* 12, 100223. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cles.2025.100223 —
quantities are from the paper's Table 1 / supplementary Table S1
(``...-mmc1.xlsx``); the search queries below are seeded from the exact
ecoinvent process names the paper cites in its own OpenLCA contribution
breakdown (``...-mmc2.xlsx``), then re-verified against this project's
ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos database.

Why this inventory exists
The battery used to be ecoinvent's ``market for battery, Li-ion, LFP,
rechargeable, prismatic`` [GLO]: an **electric-vehicle traction pack**
(Dai et al. / GREET lineage, 2016-era, 116 Wh/kg) with no container, racking,

DC block's carbon in every source that itemises them.

bw:373057708044136455.comment: Voß ESI Table S36, the weight distribution of Fraunhofer FFB's large prismatic cell. The table repeats its first two rows after the material block (ESI p. 27; cap sheet 0.204, busbar copper 0.061/0.062); they are taken once, which is what makes the rows sum to 0.987 kg per kg as printed rather than 1.25. ASSUMED: the whole 330 g is charged on this table. Voß say fixing and isolation materials (Table S37, all PET) are part of the housing but give no split, and S36 already carries PET; putting part of the 330 g on S37 instead would lower the housing. The in-China lorry leg is kept; the sea and European legs are not taken.

bw:371707331893866498.name: Solar inverter-station step-up transformer replacements, 30 years, per MWp of PV connected
bw:371707331893866498.product: 30 years of solar step-up transformer replacements, per MWp
bw:371707331893866498.comment: Smith 2024 Table A15 charges 1.30E-05 transformer replacements per m2 of module over 30 years against 4.30E-05 installed (A14): 30.2% of the fleet, the same fraction upv.py keeps for the inverters in the same row. The fraction transfers to this study's unit and count where Smith's absolute number (for his 2.7 MVA A11 unit) would not. Functional unit is 30 years of replacements for 1 MWp of PV CONNECTED; transformers.py charges it per year, independently of the life the unit itself is amortised over. In since 21 Oct 2026; the wind step-ups have no replacement rate because Leng publish none (an unsourced flow, registered for the cut-off test). Same boundary as the unit: no delivery to site, no end-of-life.
bw:371707331893866498.source:
Power transformers — Leng et al. 2026 (wind step-ups and the grid intake),
IEA PVPS 2026 (solar step-ups).

Why this inventory exists
A wind turbine generates at **690 V**, which is *low* voltage (<1 kV, the band
ecoinvent itself draws). A PV inverter's terminals are 400 V. The data centre
draws at *medium* voltage, 1–24 kV, because that is the level ``market for
electricity, medium voltage`` describes and the level the Zhang foreground is
authored against. Something has to bridge those, and it is not optional:
100 MW at 690 V is 83,674 A, which is not a cable. So every turbine carries its
own transformer at the foot of its tower — one per turbine, not one per farm —
and every PV inverter station carries one.

bw:371707331893866496.name: Wind turbine step-up transformers, per MW of wind connected
bw:371707331893866496.comment: The transformers at the foot of each turbine tower, which step 690 V (LOW, <1 kV) up to the site collection voltage so the data centre can draw at MEDIUM voltage (1-24 kV). One unit per TURBINE, not one per farm. Not optional: 100 MW at 690 V is 83,674 A. ecoinvent 3.9.1 has no power transformer at any rating - its four transformer activities are two electronic components of 280 g and 30 g average weight, by its own comments - and its wind turbine dataset lists its parts as Rotor/Nacelle/Electronics/Tower/Foundation with no transformer among them, its only electrical item being 438.7 kg of control electronics. So this is assembled from Leng et al. (2026), Processes 14(7) 1045, Supplementary Table S1: the 50 x 2.2 MVA S11-2200/35 box transformers on their 100 MW Gaoyou farm, 282,343 kg in total, divided by the farm. Cross-checked against Teffera et al. (2021) Int J LCA 26:76-96 Table 5, which lands within the same band by a different route. Functional unit is 1 MW of wind CONNECTED - amortise over TX_ASSET_LIFE_YEARS (dc_config). INCLUDES Leng Table S3's box-transformer foundations (since 21 Oct 2026) and electrical installation - section steel, terminal blocks, welding rod, lead seals (since 22 Oct 2026), per MW of the same farm. EXCLUDES: the grid-export transformer (this study is behind the meter, there is nothing to export into, and the grid intake is charged by grid_connection.py); any step between the collection network and the data centre (both sit in the medium-voltage band); switchgear and protection; losses; end-of-life. Leng publish no factory energy for the unit, so none is charged.

bw:371707331893866497.name: Solar inverter-station step-up transformers, per MWp of PV connected
bw:371707331893866497.comment: The oil-immersed transformers in a utility PV plant's inverter stations, stepping the inverters' 400 V (LOW, <1 kV) up to the site collection voltage so the data centre can draw at MEDIUM voltage (1-24 kV). The source unit is wound 20/0.4 kV, which is TX_SITE_COLLECTION_KV (20 kV) exactly, so no voltage adjustment is applied - unlike the wind units, which are wound for 35 kV and whose mass therefore errs high. ecoinvent 3.9.1 has no power transformer at any rating, so this is assembled from a published bill of materials: IEA PVPS Task 12, Report T12-33:2026 (July 2026), Tables 49 and 50. Table 49 gives one 2.5 MVA unit at 5,680 kg; Table 50 puts 4 of them on the 10 MWp reference plant, so the count is READ OFF at 0.4 units/MWp rather than derived - which retires the ASSUMED SOLAR_DC_AC_RATIO and POWER_FACTOR the old path needed. The magnetic core is grain-oriented electrical steel, disaggregated by the source into converter-route steel + MG-silicon + hot and cold rolling because no LCI database carries a GOES dataset. The workbook's '36.96 m3' hardboard cell is 36.96 kg mislabelled (its own comment says kg), carried as 0.0291 m3; the bill then sums to 5,670 kg against the report's 'approximately 5,680' (stepup_transformers.check). Functional unit is 1 MWp of PV CONNECTED - amortise over TX_ASSET_LIFE_YEARS (dc_config). INCLUDES factory electricity and heat, which the wind bill does not - process energy is ~6% here, so materials-only the two land within 1% of each other; the asymmetry is stated in SOURCES.md. INCLUDES (since 21 Oct 2026) the transformer station building from Z-PV-238, 10 m2 per unit. EXCLUDES: the grid-export transformer (behind the meter); any step between collection and the data centre (both medium voltage); switchgear and protection; losses; end-of-life.

bw:371707331902255104.name: Containerised LV step-up transformer, per MW of inverter rating (battery PCS, fuel cell)
bw:371707331902255104.comment: The transformer that steps a battery container's PCS output, or a fuel-cell container's inverter output, from LOW voltage (400 V) up to the site collection voltage (20 kV). Functional unit is 1 MW of inverter rating: transformers.py charges it per MW of cap_batt_p and per MW of cap_fc, each amortised over the asset's own life (the battery's 15 y; the fuel cell's BoP calendar life). MASS from Jasper et al. 2026, CSS (liquid cooled) bill, 'transformer, for grid connection': 5,500 kg per 1,600 kW container = 3,437.5 kg/MW, on the measured curve (2,566 kg/MVA at 2.2 MVA, 2,272 at 2.5). COMPOSITION, forming and factory energy per kg from the IEA PVPS T12-33:2026 Table 49 20/0.4 kV oil-immersed unit, a STATED SUBSTITUTION for Jasper's own recipe on technological representativeness (decided 22 Oct 2026). Jasper give a per-kg split (air-cooled sheet rows 225-236), but their §2.4.3 says it is derived from Hunziker et al. (2020): a 630 kVA line-frequency transformer with an ON-LOAD TAP CHANGER, scaled by mass to 1,800 kVA. The IEA unit is a current 2,500 kVA distribution transformer built from product documentation at exactly the 20/0.4 kV step the container needs. Jasper's recipe scores 7.85 kg CO2e/kg against 4.57 here (+72 %, mostly its 0.09 kg/kg of control electronics, likely the tap changer's); it is the sensitivity case. Closed as negligible on 4 Sep 2026 and modelled on 15 Oct: the inventory and loss machinery existed by then, and leaving it out favoured the storage chains against the generation chains, which pay for theirs. EXCLUDES: switchgear, protection and civils (as every transformer here); losses, which conversion_losses.py charges as energy; end-of-life.

bw:371707331893866499.name: Grid-intake transformer, per MVA of grid-intake transformer capacity
bw:371707331893866499.comment: The power transformer that steps the network's high voltage down onto the site, sized by cap_grid. Functional unit is 1 MVA of rating; grid_connection.py turns it into a per-MW figure with N-1 redundancy and the power factor, and amortises it over its own ASSET_LIFE_YEARS. ecoinvent 3.9.1 has no power transformer at any rating - its four transformer activities are two electronic components of 280 g and 30 g average weight, 'used in the information and communication technology' by its own comments - and no substation or switchgear dataset either. So this is assembled from Leng et al. (2026), Processes 14(7) 1045, Supplementary Table S1: the Gaoyou farm's grid-end main transformer, XZ11-100000/110, one 100 MVA unit wound for 110 kV, 71,458.6 kg in total = 714.6 kg/MVA, divided by its rating. Materials mapped exactly as the wind step-ups are, Iron read as core steel. VOLTAGE: a 110 kV unit fits a GB 132 kV EHV/DNO connection, the common case for a ~100 MW data centre; for a 275/400 kV transmission-connected site it errs LOW, supergrid transformers being heavier per MVA. Used for every site as the default. EXCLUDES: switchgear and protection (cut-off register); the line to the site (grid_connection.py reports it separately); losses; end-of-life. The switchyard's civils are their own activity, grid_intake_substation_civils_per_mw (Leng Table S3's outdoor venue, decision D2, 22 Oct 2026). Leng publish no factory energy for this unit; their 342 t CO2e against ~275 t here is a scoring difference (ecoinvent 3.11 v 3.9.1), not a dropped flow.

bw:371707331893866500.name: Grid-intake substation civils (switchyard), per MW of connection
bw:371707331893866500.comment: The civils of the intake substation's switchyard, per MW of connection: Leng et al. (2026) Table S3 'outdoor venue project' of the Gaoyou farm's 110 kV booster station - site formation, foundation beams, steel formwork, board, nails and wire, concrete, water and reinforcement, every row at the printed amount, divided by the 100 MW the station serves (decision D2, 22 Oct 2026: one yard serves both intake transformers, so it scales with the connection, not the MVA installed). Leng's own score for the venue is 2,157 t CO2e per 100 MW (34.4 % of the station). The station's buildings are covered by Zhang's facility building (stated substitution); its construction machinery is not separable and is on the cut-off register. grid_connection.py charges this per MW of cap_grid over ASSET_LIFE_YEARS. EXCLUDES switchgear, protection, delivery to site, end-of-life.

inventories.note: One database per source, written by optimiser_lca/ (python -m optimiser_lca.build).

db:solar foreground.name: solar foreground
db:solar foreground.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.

Source and scope
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

db:grid foreground.name: grid foreground
db:grid foreground.source:
GB grid electricity, 2025 annual mean, delivered at high voltage.

Source and scope
**Functional unit: 1 kWh of electricity delivered at high voltage**, on the
grid this study scores everywhere else (``optimiser_lca.grid``), as a
foreground activity, so that an inventory which takes GB grid power (the
hydrogen routes) links to it instead of ecoinvent's 2018 GB market. Every grid
kWh in the study is then on one basis.

db:hydrogen foreground.name: hydrogen foreground
db:hydrogen foreground.source:
Hydrogen production — Hermesmann & Müller 2022 (fossil routes), Gerloff 2021
(electrolysers), six routes.

Source and scope
* SMR, SMR-CCS, CCS and MP-E: Hermesmann, M. & Müller, T.E. (2022), "Green,
  Turquoise, Blue, or Grey? Environmentally friendly Hydrogen Production in
  Transforming Energy Systems", Prog. Energy Combust. Sci. 90, 100996 —
  Tables 2–3 (inventories per kg H2) and §3.2.3 (CCS). Transcribed through the
  study's own SimaPro project (SMR.XLSX, smr ccs.XLSX, ccs.XLSX); checked row
  by row against the paper on 21–22 Oct 2026.
* AE, PEM and SOEC units and operation: Gerloff, N. (2021), J. Energy Storage
  43, 102759 — SI Figures 1–5 (the 1 MW bills, every row labelled BoP or
  Stack) and Tables 3–6 (manufacturing energy, lifetime hydrogen, operating
  data). Transcribed through the same SimaPro project; checked row by row
  against the SI on 22 Oct 2026.

db:data centre foreground.name: data centre foreground
db:data centre foreground.source:
Data centre facility — Zhang et al. 2025, Virginia hyperscale.

Source and scope
Materials-production + operation inventory for a representative hyperscale
data centre (10,000 m² white space, Virginia US, SERC grid, PUE 1.4 baseline,
25-year operating life), from Zhang, M., Carbajales-Dale, M., Ma, X., Guo, L.,
Fan, C. (2025). "Cleaner grid or smarter cooling? Environmental impact
trade-offs of a data center using the life cycle assessment method." *Cleaner
Energy Systems* 12, 100223. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cles.2025.100223 —
quantities are from the paper's Table 1 / supplementary Table S1
(``...-mmc1.xlsx``); the search queries below are seeded from the exact
ecoinvent process names the paper cites in its own OpenLCA contribution
breakdown (``...-mmc2.xlsx``), then re-verified against this project's
ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos database.

db:battery foreground.name: battery foreground
db:battery foreground.source:
Grid-scale battery storage — Jasper et al. 2026 container, Voß et al. 2025 cell.

Why this inventory exists
The battery used to be ecoinvent's ``market for battery, Li-ion, LFP,
rechargeable, prismatic`` [GLO]: an **electric-vehicle traction pack**
(Dai et al. / GREET lineage, 2016-era, 116 Wh/kg) with no container, racking,
HVAC or fire suppression — ``battery.CONTAINER_UPLIFT_FRACTION`` was 0.0 and
said so. A grid battery is neither of those things. It is large-format
prismatic cells in racks, in a 20 ft container, with its own thermal
management and fire suppression, and those non-cell parts are 18-23 % of the
DC block's carbon in every source that itemises them.

db:hydrogen storage foreground.name: hydrogen storage foreground
db:hydrogen storage foreground.source:
Hydrogen storage tank — Gandiglio et al. 2022, a steel vessel.

Source and scope
    M. Gandiglio, P. Marocco, I. Bianco, D. Lovera, G.A. Blengini, M. Santarelli,
    "Life cycle assessment of a renewable energy system with hydrogen-battery
    storage for a remote off-grid community", Int. J. Hydrogen Energy 47 (2022)
    32822-32834. Table 5 (p. 32828): the hydrogen tank is one line, 15,652 kg of
    "Steel, chromium steel 18/8 {GLO}" for a 21.6 m³ vessel at 28 bar, over the
    plant's 25-year life, charged once.

db:transformer foreground.name: transformer foreground
db:transformer foreground.source:
Power transformers — Leng et al. 2026 (wind step-ups and the grid intake),
IEA PVPS 2026 (solar step-ups).

Why this inventory exists
A wind turbine generates at **690 V**, which is *low* voltage (<1 kV, the band
ecoinvent itself draws). A PV inverter's terminals are 400 V. The data centre
draws at *medium* voltage, 1–24 kV, because that is the level ``market for
electricity, medium voltage`` describes and the level the Zhang foreground is
authored against. Something has to bridge those, and it is not optional:
100 MW at 690 V is 83,674 A, which is not a cable. So every turbine carries its
own transformer at the foot of its tower — one per turbine, not one per farm —
and every PV inverter station carries one.

Neither `transformers.py` nor `grid_connection.py` counts switchgear, so it is a level shift rather than a bias between building and importing. Small — Teffera puts MV + HV switchgear at 0.61 t/MW against a plant transformer's 1.08 t/MW, and a site's own bays are a tiny share of the national fleet the 0.025 g CO₂e/kWh network term covers. Points the same way as the losses row below, and stacks with it. Closing it needs a switchgear EPD **and** a bay count, which is a network-design outcome like `sites.connection_limit_mw`.

This and the tank's leakage are the same parameter on opposite sides of the hydrogen-versus-battery seasonal contest, and both are still zero by default. **Bounded by sweep, 14 Oct** — battery 0 / 0.1 / 0.25 / 0.5 %/day × tank 0 / 0.01 / 0.1 %/day, both objectives, `optimisation_outputs/storage_loss_sweep.csv`. Reference case: North Norfolk, 100 MW IT at PUE 1.5, 2025, hourly, **islanded**, with wind, solar, battery, PEM electrolyser, tank and fuel cell all available (`res_h2` with the battery unlocked) — the one architecture where the two stores actually compete; every stored grid-connected run builds no electrolyser or tank at all. Across the whole grid: **min cost** £132.02–132.30m (+0.21 %), 62,542–62,665 t CO₂e (−0.04 to +0.16 %), battery 2,048–2,069 MWh, tank 187–192 t, electrolyser 5.6–5.7 MW, fuel cell 35.7–36.4 MW; **min carbon** £166.67–166.85m (+0.11 %), 53,624–53,641 t (+0.03 %), battery 217–221 MWh, tank 167.3 t, electrolyser 80.2–80.4 MW, fuel cell 119.5–119.8 MW. **No flip at any point**: the battery delivers 87 % of stored output at min cost and hydrogen 61–66 % at min carbon. It is small because both builds keep the battery nearly empty — it averages ~9 % of capacity at min cost and ~7 % at min carbon — and the model charges the loss on *stored* energy. That is the judgement to check: HVAC/BMS auxiliary load really scales with *installed* capacity, so charged that way the top of the band is ~3.75 GWh/yr at min cost, ~0.3 % of the 1.31 TWh demand — still no flip. The result is now bounded at these orders of magnitude, not open; one site, one year, perfect foresight, and taken while the grid-connection transformer rebuild was in flight (that term is zero here, islanded). Candidate sources for a value: BEIS 2022, or a BESS auxiliary-load study.

assumptions.1. Data centre runs flat at 100 %:
## 1. Data centre runs flat at 100 %

Continuous draw of **7,306 kW**. This is not an added assumption: the Zhang et
al. foreground's own operation exchange is 1.60e9 kWh over a 25-year life,
which is 7,306 kW continuous. It is where the old `dashboard_config.SYS_DC_DEMAND_MW
= 7.31` came from.

That figure is the **whole facility**, at Zhang's own PUE of 1.4, so the IT load
behind it is **5,219 kW**. The two must not be confused: `size_mw_it` is an IT
load and is multiplied by the caller's PUE to get demand, so passing 7.31 with a
PUE above 1.0 models a facility larger than Zhang's. `DC_REFERENCE_PUE` exists to
make the conversion explicit and is the only place Zhang's PUE is used — the
facility's embodied burden is anchored on IT capacity, not on facility draw, so
improving PUE no longer shrinks the building.

*Consequence*: no load-shifting option, and no diurnal or seasonal demand
shape. Storage is therefore sized purely against supply variability, never
against demand variability — which makes renewables+storage look somewhat
harder than it would with a flexible AI training load.
assumptions.2. Geography is GB, via the electricity:
## 2. Geography is GB, via the electricity exchange

The data centre foreground is authored in Virginia against `market for
electricity, medium voltage [US-SERC]`. Rather than re-authoring the
inventory, that electricity is swapped for the half-hourly GB grid mix from the
Carbon Intensity API (`optimisation/grid_build.py`, originally notebook 3.1),
by the exact `fixed + Σ kWh×EF` decomposition in `baseline_grid.py`.

The inventory has **exactly one** electricity exchange — IT + cooling/aux,
1.60e9 kWh over 25 years — and it is the only US-*grid* input in the activity
(the concrete is RNA, i.e. North American, as the audit noted).
The swap is applied two ways, which agree to 1e-4 %: the full Brightway
substitution above, and the `fixed + Σ kWh×EF` decomposition
`baseline_grid.py` uses so the optimiser can treat the facility as linear
coefficients.

*Residual*: the remaining twelve exchanges are **global-market** datasets —
`GLO` for reinforcing and structural steel, copper, aluminium, tap water, the
diesel genset, the UPS battery and R134a; `RoW` for PUR foam and sodium
hypochlorite. So they are not US-specific, but they are not GB-specific either,
and no transport leg is modelled at all. Together with the materials they are
about 963 t CO2e/y charged at the reference facility (14 Oct 2026, after the
refrigerant leakage was added), plus the 32.5 t genset the LP excludes.
Sourcing them to GB/European supply chains is a known, unmodelled refinement.
The R134a top-up is also emitted as HFC-134a: Zhang derive it as leakage
replacement (see SOURCES.md).

*Scope*: the activity is **Material Production + Construction + Operation**
(construction energy and water in since 21 Oct 2026: they are in the source
and inside the boundary). Transportation (delivery to site), disposal and
recycling are outside the boundary — so the facility carries no
decommissioning or demolition burden. See §6. Zhang's own figures put the
facility at 7.53 MW with 5.38 MW of IT; the 7,306 / 5,219 kW read out of the
1.60e9 kWh they print sit 3 % under those (7.53 MW × 8,760 h × 25 y is 1.649e9,
printed rounded down). The energy-driven part is charged per MWh of that printed
electricity, so it is unaffected. The IT-driven part (servers, UPS, building,
construction) was sized on 5.38 MW of IT, so since 26 Oct 2026 it is normalised
by 5.38 MW, not by the 5.219 MW read back (`data_centre.ZHANG_IT_MW`; it was 3.1 %
high per MW of IT before). Zhang's §2.2b names chillers, cooling towers, pumps and
piping as in scope but S1 does not disaggregate them, and the 2,000 kg initial
R134a charge is a sizing note, not an inventory row: both are taken as inside
Zhang's own rows and not added (user, 26 Oct 2026).
assumptions.3. Hydrogen the study *makes* is co-loca:
## 3. Hydrogen the study *makes* is co-located with its use; hydrogen it *buys* is compressed but not hauled

No hydrogen transport, distribution or liquefaction is modelled, for any
hydrogen pathway — green, grey, blue or turquoise. Self-production assumes a
plant adjacent to the data centre, feeding the fuel cell (or the storage tank)
directly at the plant gate.

**Delivery compression is no longer excluded.** It used to be, on the same
co-location argument — but that argument covers hydrogen this study produces and
not hydrogen it purchases, which by definition comes from somebody else's plant.
Meanwhile self-produced hydrogen was charged a compression parasitic to enter
the tank and bought hydrogen was not, so the exclusion was also an asymmetry
that favoured buying. Every bought colour now carries the work of compressing it
to 200 bar tube-trailer pressure at the seller's gate, in both objectives —
`h2_prices.bought_h2_compression_*`, detailed in `SOURCES.md`. Road haulage
itself is still excluded, and is registered in `DATA_GAPS.md` rather than
justified here.

*Verified*: no H2 distribution exchange exists in `hydrogen foreground`,
`fuel cell foreground` or `hydrogen storage foreground`, so nothing is being
double-counted. The two transport exchanges that do exist are unrelated —
CO2-to-storage pipeline inside the CCS chain, and the negative passenger-car
term that removes ecoinvent's domestic-micro-CHP service-visit artefact.

*Consequence*: the SMR / SMR-CCS / MP-E options implicitly site a reformer or
pyrolysis unit on the data centre campus, fed from the gas grid. Plausible at
this scale, but it is an assumption, not a finding. The "off-site green
hydrogen" option is now "green hydrogen bought at a price, with its production
burden and its compression, but no haulage".

Storage compression is still counted where it applies, via
`h2_storage.compression_kwh_per_kg` from the electrolyser's delivery pressure
to the tank's — zero for the 28 bar design, since the electrolyser already
delivers at ~30 bar.

**Bought green hydrogen is green by definition, and that rests on certificates.**
Decided 2–3 Sep. The grid-connected share of bought green
(`h2_prices.GREEN_H2_GRID_SHARE`, 0.5) is scored on a *renewable* electricity
basis plus the grid's high-voltage delivery terms — 1.107 kg CO₂e/kg against
0.976 behind the meter — not on the grid mix the electrolyser physically draws from. That is a
market-based reading, and it holds only if the seller's grid electricity is
backed by matched renewable certificates (REGOs, or an RFNBO-style hourly match).
Two things follow that the numbers do not show on their own:

- The price carries **no certificate premium**. NESO's and EHO's grid-connected
  LCOH are priced on wholesale power, so the bought-green price is the cost of
  the electricity, not of the claim to it.
- The LP's **own** grid electrolyser (`grid_h2`) is scored on the real
  location-based grid mix instead. Same physical setup, two bases: about
  **8.8 kg CO₂e/kg** made on site at London's 2025 annual mean against **1.06**
  bought. The asymmetry favours
  buying, and it is deliberate — the study assumes a buyer can contract for
  certified green hydrogen but does not assume the data centre certifies its own
  imports. Anyone comparing `grid_h2` with bought green should read the gap as
  partly an accounting convention, not only physics. Audit §3.6.
assumptions.2b. Grid carbon is an average, attributi:
## 2b. Grid carbon is an average, attributional, life-cycle figure

**Average, not marginal.** Every grid import is charged the half-hour's
*average* life-cycle intensity of the region's generation mix, never the
marginal plant's. That is the attributional reading, and it matches every
other coefficient in the study: an asset is charged its own inventory, not the
change it causes elsewhere. A marginal (consequential) factor answers a
different question — what the system emits *because* the data centre draws one
more kWh — and would change what avoiding an import is worth: Hawkes puts GB's
long-run marginal at 0.26–0.53 kg CO₂/kWh now against a 0.69 short-run, both
well above today's average. Using it would need a consequential treatment of
every asset as well, so it is out of scope, and the Overview lists it as an
extension. Which way it would move the answer is not one-signed — a marginal
factor values an avoided import differently and swings differently across the
day — so this is recorded as a limitation, not a bias of known direction.

**Delivered at the connection voltage.** A kWh imported carries the losses and
the network's embodied carbon down to the voltage the site connects at
(`optimiser_lca.grid.DELIVERY`, ecoinvent's GB voltage chain). Every site this
study prices connects at high voltage — transmission, or an EHV distribution
band — so imports pay ×1.0338 on generation plus 1.93 g/kWh. A bought-hydrogen
seller's grid electricity is delivered on the same constants
(`h2_prices.GREEN_H2_SELLER_VOLTAGE`), so the two grid users share one basis.

**Imports follow the flows that reach the region.** The API reports a region's
imports as one figure. It is split across exporting countries each half-hour by
Elexon's interconnector flows, weighted by a per-region attribution fitted to
NESO's own regional import share (`optimiser_lca.grid.IMPORT_ATTRIBUTION`). The
fit is a calibration to NESO's regional model, not a physical flow trace;
every exporter is scored on its own country's average HV market, not on the
plant at its margin.
assumptions.3a. The site is a coordinate, and everyt:
## 3a. The site is a coordinate, and everything follows from it

`sites.resolve(lat, lon)` derives the Carbon Intensity region and the TNUoS
demand zone from the coordinate, so the weather, the grid mix and the network
bill cannot drift apart from one another. Two real lookups
(postcodes.io → Carbon Intensity API) plus a fixed GSP-group correspondence for
the TNUoS zone, checked against presets set independently from published
sources.

*Consequence, and it is a correction*: the old `dashboard_config.WIND_LAT / WIND_LON`
(51.7320, -0.3711) is a field near **St Albans** — Carbon Intensity region 10,
TNUoS zone 9. Every cached grid series in this repo is **region 13, London**,
TNUoS zone 12. So the study as it previously stood paired London's grid carbon
intensity and London's £7.41/kW demand tariff with a Hertfordshire wind site.

Carbon-wise the two regions are similar and the error is small. The network
charge is not: zone 12 is £7.41/kW against zone 9's £1.11/kW. Nothing warned
about it because nothing connected the wind coordinate to the grid region.
`require_grid_region()` now refuses the combination outright, and the matrix is
run at a coordinate genuinely inside region 13.
assumptions.3b. Every half-hourly series is on UTC:
## 3b. Every half-hourly series is on UTC

Grid carbon, wholesale price and wind/solar are joined on naive UTC timestamps,
and a requested window is read as UTC. Until 12 Oct 2026 the grid series was
London local time while price and weather were UTC, so from late March to late
October intraday grid carbon sat an hour late against everything else (Audit
§3.5). Every saved grid file was rebuilt on UTC that day and carries a
`clock = UTC` column; `profiles.py` ignores grid files without it.

Rules published on the UK clock convert from UTC where they are applied: the
DUoS red/amber/green bands (`network_charges.duos_band`) and Elexon settlement
periods (`grid_build.normalise_elexon`). The DUoS bands run all year (red
weekdays 11:00–14:00 and 16:00–19:00), so in summer every band moves by an hour.
assumptions.3c. Generation is onshore wind and groun:
## 3c. Generation is onshore wind and ground-mount solar only

Every site is on land (decided 3 Sep), so offshore wind is out of scope and
`dc_architectures.OFFSHORE_IN_SCOPE` holds it off for every architecture and
every caller. It used to be unlocked wherever `sites.Site.offshore_wind` flagged
a coastal region, and the LP has no offshore profile — `cap_offshore` ran on the
*onshore* capacity-factor series, so in the high cost case it built offshore on
onshore yield. The offshore coefficients are still built and reported; turning
the switch back on needs an offshore series first.
assumptions.4. Cost basis:
## 4. Cost basis

DESNZ/Arup 2024 Cost of Electricity reports, **2023 real prices**, with each
technology's own pre-tax real hurdle rate (onshore wind 5.8 %, offshore wind
6.2 %, solar PV 5.0 %) rather than a single project WACC. Set
`optimisation.tech_costs.DISCOUNT_RATE_OVERRIDE` to impose one rate instead.

*One asymmetry, deliberate*: generation step-up transformers
(`transformers.py`) are charged in **carbon and not in cost**. The DESNZ/Arup
capex is plant-plus-connection-to-the-point-of-connection, so it already
contains the electrical balance of plant; a separate £/MW transformer charge
would double count, while the carbon side has no such term anywhere — none of
the generation inventories contains a transformer, and ecoinvent has no power
transformer at any rating to supply one. See SOURCES.md.

Electricity is priced at the Elexon APXMIDP half-hourly wholesale price plus
the demand-side network charges `network_charges.py` builds (TNUoS, BSUoS,
DUoS) and, since 28 Oct 2026, the FY2026/27 policy levies and losses
`levies.py` builds: RO, FiT, CfD, AAHEDC, Nuclear RAB and CCL as one flat
£/MWh, the Capacity Market levy on its 16:00–19:00 winter working-day window,
and wholesale and BSUoS grossed up for losses: the site's own area's line loss
factor for the connection voltage and time period, times the offtaking
transmission loss multiplier for its zone and season (1 + zonal TLF read from
Elexon's 2026/27 report charts + an assumed national adjustment of 0.011).
**Assumed**: the site holds no Climate Change Agreement (`CCL_UNDER_CCA`;
with one, CCL falls from £7.75 to £0.62/MWh). Supplier margin is not included.
The connection and UoS figures in the DESNZ tables are *generator*-side and
are not a substitute.

**The national grid's location charge** (HH locational TNUoS) is charged on winter-evening demand, as the tariff is: the most the site imports in any weekday half-hour from 16:30 to 18:30, November to February, the window every Triad of the last seven winters fell in. A battery or fuel cell that covers that window saves it; the charge for the connection itself (DUoS capacity, connection capital) stays on the connection size.

**One tariff year.** Every network charge — TNUoS, the residual and its band
boundaries, BSUoS and every area's DUoS — is the **2026/27** tariff (`network_charges.TARIFF_FY`),
applied to whatever weather and wholesale window is solved. The levies are 2026/27
too (`levies.LEVY_FY`) since 28 Oct 2026.

**Where the connection runs to** (since 29 Oct 2026): the nearest substation at the connection voltage in the substation register, with the cable priced on the straight-line distance times an **assumed 1.3** route factor (no UK figure found). If the substation's published spare capacity is below the connection the run is flagged, and both routes round it are reported; the model builds at the nearest substation unless `shortfall_route="next"`. A 33 or 132 kV site's local network charges are set for its own nearest price node plus its area's **calibrated** add-on (`ehv_charges`), except in SSEN's two areas, which charged outside the method for 2026/27 and keep the listed-site median.

**The connection voltage** of a distribution site is the lowest its area's DNO connects it at, by that DNO's own published rule where there is one (`network_charges.AREA_RULES`): 11 kV up to 12 MVA by default (15 in the North West, under 8 in London), then 33 kV (up to 120 MVA, and always in Scotland), then 132 kV up to 240 MVA (250 in the NGED areas). Where a DNO publishes nothing the default stands in, and says so. Since 29 Oct 2026 that rule is the **floor**: with the site's coordinates the area's own substation capacities decide above it — where every substation within 60 km at the rule's voltage that publishes a spare capacity is short of the connection, the site connects a voltage up (`substations.voltage_with_room`), provided at least half of them publish one (an **assumed** threshold). Sizes the rules leave open can be solved both ways — an option, not the default. An 11 kV site takes HV residual bands and its grid electricity at medium voltage; 33 and 132 kV sites take EHV bands and high voltage.

**The connection ceiling** is 1 / 0.70 = **1.43x** the flat load (`sites.CONNECTION_HEADROOM_ASSUMED`): the 70 % data-centre load factor of the national energy scenarios (FES Pathway Assumptions 2025, as applied in NGED's Data Centre Impact Study, Nov 2025). Until 29 Oct 2026 it was 1.5x, assumed. The page's headroom box overrides it.

**The substation register's capacity layer** (since 30 Oct 2026, `scripts/register_capacity.py`) takes each company's own published figure on the company's own basis, and says which: "firm capacity minus maximum demand" (the standard capacity heatmaps), "headroom on connected demand" (National Grid's opportunity map, which also publishes headroom net of contracted demand), with the portal's date on every row. Those bases are not identical across companies, and the dates run from March 2025 to October 2026 — the register reports this rather than levelling it. Joins between a company's datasets are by its own site id, then by name at a compatible level, then by location within **300 m** (assumed radius); a 275/400 kV substation takes the nearest grid-supply-point record within **3 km** (assumed). Where no company dataset covers a row the builder's own figure stands, marked "builder". The "central" scenario for room in a future year is the company's own — Holistic Transition (UK Power Networks, Northern Powergrid), Best View (Electricity North West), HT (SSEN) — a **choice**. The availability listing (`optimisation.availability`) prices every candidate for a flat load at the connection ceiling with the site at the substation, so the cable is the default **2 km** route and the wholesale price the 2025 mean: it ranks places by what the grid costs there, not by what the optimiser would build. **Price nodes** are used only where the schedule's node was matched by name to the connection substation itself (decision of 30 Oct 2026); place-name and code placements are still built and reported but no longer price a run. **Room is checked at the connecting substation only** (a known limitation, decided 30 Oct 2026): a primary with room may sit under a bulk or grid supply point that has none, so room is overstated for 11 kV sites (up to about 10 MW IT); sites of 30 MW IT and above connect at the bulk or grid supply point itself and are barely affected, and SSEN's figures already include the limit above. Checking the chain was judged not worth it yet: parents are named by every company, but the figures at the level above are patchy (none at National Grid's grid supply points).

**The connection tier** follows GB's voltage rule, not a size threshold: a DNO
connects demand up to 240 MVA in England and Wales and up to 120 MVA in
Scotland, where 132 kV is transmission (ENWL ES216; the Scottish figure is a
proxy). Above that the site is transmission-connected and pays no DUoS. Below it the site
pays its own area's DUoS (`duos_areas`): an 11 kV site its area's HV Site Specific
row, a 33 or 132 kV site the median of its area's listed EHV sites in the same
band, each in that area's own time bands, and its area's line loss factors.
`Site.transmission_connected` overrides the rule — a real connection offer
beats it. Until 30 Oct 2026 the TDR band was read from the connection ceiling
and the built connection held inside that band (`floor ≤ cap_grid ≤ ceiling`;
the floor one kVA above the band below's inclusive top since 29 Oct 2026). In
the 14-area check of 29 Oct 2026 the floor bound in 29 of 42 runs, every
England-and-Wales 150 MW IT site at the transmission boundary, and solved both
ways the local network was £6.5–11.5 m/yr cheaper — which is why the band is
now chosen in the LP (next paragraph). The single-list model is kept as
`connection_mode="single"`.

**The price list is chosen by the optimiser** (since 30 Oct 2026,
`connection_options.py`, COST_PLAN §1.11). Every price list the site could be
on — national grid or local network, voltage, residual band, at a named
substation — is an option with a size range, its own cable and charges, and
one on/off switch; exactly one is on, and the connection size is chosen with
it, comparing the whole site's cost (or carbon). Imports take one series per
voltage group (national grid, 132 kV, 33 kV, 11 kV) with that voltage's
losses, unit rates and delivered carbon. What is **assumed or simplified**
here: (i) in the default **room mode** each option is capped by *today's*
published room at its substation, on the company's own basis and date — room
is a hard limit, not a forecast, and room after agreed connections or in a
future year is reported only; (ii) a substation that publishes **no figure is
skipped** for the nearest at that voltage that does, and where that one has
less room than the load the **next substation with room** is a second option
at its own cable length — so a blank is neither "full" nor "unlimited"; (iii)
the published size rule still decides between 11 kV and the voltages above (a
connection within the area's 11 kV limit is an 11 kV one), and the **national
grid option starts at the company's largest local connection** (240/250 MVA,
120 in Scotland), the tier rule of 28 Oct 2026; the choice therefore runs
from 33 kV up, and a national-grid connection *below* that top — which NGED's
study says is also possible — is not offered; (iv) the bands at one voltage
share that voltage's **unit rates**, taken from the band the load itself falls
in, an approximation only where an area's 33/132 kV unit rates differ by band
(the listed-site medians); (v) the "next with room" option takes the nearest
substation's price node for its site-specific charges; (vi) in the **cap
mode** every option is capped at one figure that ignores room — 1.43x the
load or the cap entered — and only the nearest substation at each voltage is
offered. `Site.transmission_connected` and `Site.tdr_band` still narrow the
options to that tier or band; `Site.connection_limit_mw` is the cap mode with
that cap. With one option left, or in the single mode, the model is exactly
the one before this change.

**No room nearby is an answer, not a connection** (30 Oct 2026, afternoon).
A published room of zero is a figure — the place is full — so an option it
would cap at 0 MW is dropped, not kept as a free standing charge. The search
for a substation with room has a **reach per voltage**
(`substations.REACH_KM`: 5 km at 11 kV, 15 km at 33 kV, 40 km at 132 kV, 60 km
to the national grid; rules of thumb, **assumed**), because beyond that the
engineering answer is the next voltage up, not a longer cable; the
single-price-list model keeps its 60 km. When no price list survives at any
voltage — everything in reach is full, publishes nothing, or does not exist —
`build_series` raises `ConnectionUnavailable` instead of inventing a 1.43x
connection, and the page asks "No room found nearby: run islanded?"; an
islanded run is then the site served every hour from what is built on it,
with no standby generator. **The cable is now in carbon as well as cost**
(30 Oct 2026, afternoon): the line to the connection substation is charged
per option over its own route, two circuits, over the line's 40-year life, as
a fixed carbon term on the option's switch (`ConnectionOption.gwp_fixed_per_year`;
`Tech.gwp_grid_fixed_per_year` with one price list). Until then an option
with a long cable was dearer in money and free in carbon. The figure is
ecoinvent's high-voltage transmission network per km — an overhead line's
towers and conductors — standing in for a buried 33/132 kV cable, so a
**proxy**, probably high: 8.7 t CO₂e per km per year, which makes a 5 km
two-circuit cable 87 t a year, the carbon of about 370 MW of intake
transformers, and 0.1–0.2 % of a 150 MW IT site's total. What the model still cannot see: that "full" is
usually a *date* (reinforcement below the high-cost cap costs the customer
time, not money), the price of reinforcement above the cap, and a flexible
(curtailable) connection — all listed as open in COST_PLAN §1.11.

**The connection's capital** (`connection_cost.py`) is charged on the same
split as its carbon: the intake substation per MW of `cap_grid` and the cable
to the network as a fixed annual cost, annualised the way CUSC Section 14
charges connection assets. Under the Access SCR a demand customer pays for its
extension assets only, so no reinforcement contribution is added. Since 29 Oct
2026 the prices are the site's own DNO's (eleven areas on their own 2026
connection charging statements); a row a company prints as POA takes the
**median of the lists that publish it** and is named as a stand-in. NGED's
substation rows are kept for its four areas and **flagged low** (4–5x below
the other publishers: transformers and switchgear without civils and land).
assumptions.5. Emissions are IPCC 2021 GWP100, attri:
## 5. Emissions are IPCC 2021 GWP100, attributional

Grid electricity uses the **average** attributional intensity of the regional
mix, not short-run marginal intensity. This is the right basis for reporting
the facility's footprint; it is the wrong basis for claiming that shifting a
load reduces real-world emissions. Any timing-based result should be reported
against both.

**No credits anywhere; co-products carry no burden away.** Decided 21 Oct
2026. The study takes no avoided-burden credits: not for recycling (§6), and
not for co-products. Two cases in the inventories: methane pyrolysis, where
Hermesmann & Müller credit the 3 kg of solid carbon per kg H₂ against carbon
black, and SMR / SMR-CCS, where they credit the excess electricity (1.10 and
0.05 kWh per kg) as an avoided burden — the second was carried "as the source
does" until 22 Oct 2026 and is now dropped too (+1.4 % on grey). Here the whole
burden sits on the hydrogen. Electrolysis oxygen is likewise an unallocated
co-product. This keeps the study attributional throughout, at the cost of
making turquoise hydrogen look worse than its source reports.
assumptions.6. No end-of-life, anywhere:
## 6. No end-of-life, anywhere

The study is **cradle-to-gate on every input**, with the functional unit being
the data centre powered at a given size, year and location. Nothing is followed
past the site gate on the way out: no demolition, decommissioning, disposal or
recycling, and no recycling credit, for the facility or for any energy asset.

**Transport to site is outside the boundary, and nothing else is.** No capital
good, cable or hydrogen is carried to the site, for any technology, because
where the site will be is not known. Transport further up the supply chain does
not depend on the site and is kept: ecoinvent's market transport, legs between
manufacturing stages, materials to a factory.

Every foreground already meets this without modification:

| Foreground | Position |
|---|---|
| Data centre | Material production, construction and operation; transportation (delivery to site), disposal and recycling outside the boundary |
| H2 storage tank | Shell, its forming, frame and pad; valves and compressor hardware on the cut-off register; end-of-life out |
| Grid connection | Transformer materials (Leng 2026's 100 MVA, 110 kV main transformer, per MVA, × 2 for N-1) and the switchyard's civils per MW of connection (Leng's outdoor venue, D2), plus a line term reported but not charged per MW; switchgear, protection and manufacturing energy carried as cut-off estimates (§8); losses in the LP; no end-of-life |
| Generation step-up transformers | Transformer capital (wind materials-only; solar with IEA PVPS process energy); no switchgear, protection or civils. Losses are charged as energy in the LP (`conversion_losses.py`), not as a coefficient |
| Battery and fuel-cell step-ups (15 Oct) | Jasper 2026's container transformer mass on the IEA PVPS composition (with its process energy), a stated substitution for Jasper's own Hunziker-derived recipe on representativeness (SOURCES.md, 22 Oct), per MW of inverter rating, over the asset's own life; no switchgear, protection or civils. Losses in the LP at ASSUMED loadings (0.5 battery, 1.0 fuel cell), the fuel cell's unit energised on standby |
| Grid battery | Jasper/Voß cradle-to-gate manufacture including the cell factory's energy and upstream transport; Jasper's EOL sheet not taken, his delivery-to-site rows left out (Voß's legs to a German factory not taken, and subtracted where folded into a factor), no foundation |
| Electrolysers | Capital good plus consumables; no end-of-life exchange |
| Fuel cell stack | Babatunde et al. cradle-to-gate manufacture, no use or end-of-life phase |
| Fuel cell BoP / maintenance | Usai et al. 2021 process loops + inverter + container, cradle-to-gate; service consumables only. No end-of-life, no delivery transport |

The SMR-CCS chain's "CCS waste treatment" activity is **not** an exception: it
is the capture and storage leg of a production route, inside the gate.

*Residual, and it cannot be declared away*: coefficients scored on **ecoinvent
3.9.1 apos** carry end-of-life inside their background datasets, because the
APOS system model allocates waste-treatment burdens back into the product
system. This affects the wind, offshore, battery pack, inverter, transformer
and tank-steel terms, and cannot be stripped exchange-by-exchange from outside.
The cut-off system model is the one that corresponds to a strict cradle-to-gate
rule; moving to it would break the "3.9.1 apos throughout" consistency claim and
every pinned constant, so the embedded share is declared here rather than
removed.
assumptions.7. The facility's standby generator is e:
## 7. The facility's standby generator is excluded

Zhang's inventory carries a diesel standby generator — 8.6e6 MJ over the life,
**32.5 t CO2e/yr** at his facility size. It is scored, reported by
`dc_inputs.data_centre_coefficients()` as
`backup_kgco2e_per_year_excluded`, and **left out of every objective**.

Backup is a *decision variable* in this study: the optimiser sizes a fuel cell,
a battery, a grid connection and an unserved-energy allowance to provide exactly
the resilience the genset provides. Charging Zhang's genset on top would bill
every architecture for a second backup system, and would bill the islanded ones
twice over for a function they were built to supply.

*Consequence*: the grid-connected baselines lose an asset a real site would
probably have. The number is preserved rather than deleted so it can be added
back for a like-for-like comparison against a conventional facility.

The UPS battery is **not** treated this way and stays in. Ride-through over
seconds is a different function from bulk storage, so it is not a double count.

assumptions.8. Cut-off rule:
## 8. Cut-off rule

A flow that is in a held source and inside the boundary is always in; the
boundary excludes only end-of-life, delivery to site and the standby generator
(§6–7). The cut-off test below applies to flows no held source itemises: each
may stay out only if its upper estimate is under 1% of its technology's
carbon (rule 1), all of a technology's together under 5% (rule 2), and
adding them all back must not change the best design (rule 3, the `cutoff`
sensitivity knob). Criteria after PAS 2050 and Vestas V162 §3.3, applied per
technology; rule 3 is this study's addition under ISO 14044's sensitivity
requirement for comparative assertions. Not ecoinvent's "cut-off" system model.
Battery power-side flows are tested at a 1 h floor; energy-side flows at their
ceiling. A flow that fails is included (status below). Register:
`optimiser_lca/exclusions.py`; this section is generated by
`python optimisation/cutoff.py --write`.

The two reference cases re-solved at both anchors with every still-excluded flow added at its

central model. Q4's test: the same technologies are built and no built capacity moves by more than

| islanded_h2 | min_gwp | batt_e, batt_p, ely, fc, solar, tank, wind | yes | batt_e -1.1% | 63,828 → 64,148 | pass |

**Rule 3 passes**: at both anchors of both cases the upper-estimate run builds the same technologies and moves no capacity by more than 5 %.

The London case was solved with the grid connection at 282.0 kg CO2e per MW per year; the switchyard's

system, so it cannot move a design. The islanded case has no grid connection.

nodes.rating: 2.2 MVA box transformer, one per turbine (1.1 MVA per MW)
nodes.model: Losses applied in the LP: availability × (1 − load loss), plus no-load at the bus. The site collects at 20 kV (ASSUMED, inside the 1–24 kV band the data centre draws at), so this is a 0.69/20 kV unit. Its carbon is Leng's S11-2200/35, wound for 35 kV, used as the proxy: heavier per MVA, so it errs high. No further 35 → 20 kV step exists in the chain.
nodes.loss: no-load 0.071 % of capacity; load 0.68 % at full loading ≈ 0.30 % of output
nodes.term: Wind step-up transformers (0.69 → 20 kV, one per turbine)
nodes.source: Leng et al. 2026 Table S1 (S11-2200/35); Commission Regulation (EU) No 548/2014 (retained), Annex I, Tier 2, Tables I.1 and I.7; legislation.gov.uk, read 14 Oct 2026

nodes.name: Array collection cables, 20 kV
nodes.rating: underground MV cables, turbine to site bus, at 20 kV (ASSUMED)
nodes.model: Losses: inside the net factor's electrical term (0.98). Vestas's LCAs put electrical losses at 2.5 % to the connection point, cables and transformers together; the step-up's share is charged separately above, leaving 2 % for the cables. Carbon: inside ecoinvent's 'wind turbine network connection, 2MW' dataset, a capital good in the wind coefficient.
nodes.source: Vestas V136/V150/V162 LCAs §3.4.2; ecoinvent 3.9.1 wind turbine network connection

nodes.name: GB generators and interconnectors
nodes.rating: GB-wide 2025 mix: wind 32%, gas 28%, nuclear 13%, biomass 8%, solar 6%; imports 12.5% (FR 6.6%, NO 2.7%, DK 1.2%, BE 1.1%, NL 0.8%, IE 0.1%)
nodes.model: Shown GB-wide; the LP uses the site's own region (London, region 13) half-hour by half-hour from the Carbon Intensity API, which sets ci[t]. The LP chooses imp[t] each half-hour up to cap_grid.
nodes.source: NESO Carbon Intensity API; Elexon FUELHH

nodes.name: Transmission network, 400 / 275 / 132 kV
nodes.rating: national grid plus HVDC links
nodes.model: A gross-up on every imported kWh's carbon, and its losses: the kWh generated per kWh delivered at high voltage.
nodes.loss: ×1.0338 generated per kWh delivered (3.38 % losses); network carbon 1.93 g/kWh
nodes.source: optimiser_lca.grid.DELIVERY, from ecoinvent's GB voltage chain

nodes.name: Connection line
nodes.rating: 2 km (ASSUMED, site-specific)
nodes.model: Reported but not charged per MW; its losses are not applied.

nodes.name: Connection point and import meter
nodes.rating: cap_grid ≤ load × 1.43 (connection ceiling: 1 / the FES 70 % data-centre load factor); a connection above 100 MW counts as transmission-connected (ASSUMED)
nodes.model: imp[t] ≤ cap_grid. Imports are priced and scored here, on the grid side of the intake. Export is switched off (refused until modelled).

nodes.name: Grid intake transformers, 110/132 → 20 kV
nodes.rating: 2 MVA per MW of connection (N-1, power factor 1), charged per MVA on Leng's 100 MVA unit
nodes.model: Losses applied in the LP: delivered = (1 − load loss) × imp, no-load drawn at the bus.
nodes.loss: no-load 0.092 % of the connection; load 0.072 % of imports (k_PEI 0.4, loading 0.5 ASSUMED)
nodes.source: Leng et al. 2026 XZ11-100000/110; Commission Regulation (EU) No 548/2014 (retained), Annex I, Tier 2, Tables I.1 and I.7; legislation.gov.uk, read 14 Oct 2026

nodes.name: Liquid cooling, HVAC, BMS
nodes.rating: auxiliary load of the container
nodes.model: Its electricity is a standing loss on the stored energy: 0 by default, swept 0–0.5 %/day.

nodes.name: LFP DC block — cells, modules, racks
nodes.rating: 3,008 kWh per container = 8 racks × 8 modules × 47 kWh; 383.4 Wh cells
nodes.model: cap_batt_e is usable energy (90 % of nameplate). soc[t] ≤ cap_batt_e, cyclic over the window.
nodes.term: Battery cells, racks and container (energy capacity)
nodes.source: Jasper et al. 2026; Voß et al. 2025 cell

nodes.name: Power conversion system, AC ↔ DC
nodes.rating: 500 kW inverters (ecoinvent dataset)
nodes.model: cap_batt_p in MW bounds charge and discharge. Round-trip efficiency is split evenly: √0.88 = 0.938 each way.

nodes.name: Step-up transformer, 0.4 → 20 kV, one per container
nodes.rating: 1.6 MVA per 1.6 MW container (Jasper 2026)
nodes.model: Losses applied in the LP: discharge arrives at the bus net of the load loss, charge is drawn grossed up by it, and no-load is drawn on cap_batt_p every hour.
nodes.loss: no-load 0.066 % of PCS rating; load 0.38 % of throughput at x_eff 0.5 (ASSUMED)
nodes.term: Battery step-up transformers (0.4 → 20 kV, one per container)
nodes.source: Jasper et al. 2026 (mass) on IEA PVPS T12-33:2026 (composition); Reg. 548/2014 Tier 2 (losses)

nodes.name: Electrolyser power supply: transformer and rectifier
nodes.rating: AC → DC for the stack
nodes.model: Taken as inside the inventory's kWh per kg (54 for PEM), i.e. that figure is read as a system-level consumption with the rectifier included. Not verified against Gerloff's own definition; if their 54 kWh/kg is stack-only, the system draw is ~2–4 % higher.

nodes.name: Electrolyser stack — PEM (AE, SOEC selectable)
nodes.rating: PEM 54 kWh/kg at 30 bar · AE 51.8 · SOEC 42.3 kWh/kg + 5.24 kWh/kg heat
nodes.model: p_ely[t] ≤ cap_ely. Hydrogen made = p_ely ÷ (kWh/kg + compression). Can run at any part load (no unit commitment).
nodes.lp: cap_ely (MW), p_ely[t]; ely_stack_units = max(calendar, running hours / 50,000)

nodes.name: Natural gas supply
nodes.rating: GB gas network, high pressure (SOEC only)
nodes.model: Fuel for the SOEC's boiler. Bought fuel: its carbon is in the electrolyser's consumables term; it does not pass through the site bus.
nodes.source: Mehmeti et al. 2018; ecoinvent heat production, natural gas, at boiler

nodes.name: SOEC external heat: gas boiler
nodes.rating: 5.24 kWh heat per kg H₂ (SOEC only)
nodes.model: Gas boiler by default (bought fuel, carbon only). The electric-boiler scenario takes 5.29 kWh/kg from the site bus instead.

nodes.name: Compression to tank pressure
nodes.rating: PEM 30 → 28 bar: 0.00 kWh/kg · SOEC 1 → 28 bar: 2.10 kWh/kg
nodes.model: Its electricity is added to the electrolyser's kWh per kg, drawn from the bus.

nodes.name: Hydrogen tank — steel vessel
nodes.rating: 28 bar, 50 kg H₂ per 21.6 m³ vessel
nodes.model: tank[t] ≤ cap_tank (kg), cyclic. Fed by the electrolyser and by bought hydrogen; drained by the fuel cell. Drains to zero (no heel).
nodes.loss: leakage 0 /h by default (swept); leaked H₂ is charged at GWP 11.6

nodes.name: Fuel cell stack — PEM
nodes.rating: 63.2 kg H₂ per MWh AC = 47.5 % net (LHV), lifetime mean
nodes.model: p_fc[t] ≤ cap_fc; hydrogen burned = 63.2 kg × MWh. Stacks are replaced on max(calendar 10 y, 30,000 h).

nodes.name: Fuel cell balance of plant: air blower, humidifier, coolant pumps
nodes.rating: parasitic loads
nodes.model: Inside the net efficiency (the 47.5 % is net AC, after these loads).

nodes.name: Fuel cell inverter, DC → AC
nodes.rating: 500 kW units (ecoinvent dataset), in a container per 1,000 kW
nodes.model: Inside the net efficiency and the BoP carbon; not a separate variable.

nodes.name: Step-up transformer, 0.4 → 20 kV, one per container
nodes.rating: 1 MVA per 1 MW container
nodes.model: Losses applied in the LP: p_fc arrives at the bus net of the load loss; no-load is drawn on cap_fc every hour because the unit is kept energised on standby (decision, 15 Oct).
nodes.loss: no-load 0.069 % of cap_fc, always; load 0.76 % of output at x_eff 1 (ASSUMED)
nodes.term: Fuel-cell step-up transformers (0.4 → 20 kV, one per container)
nodes.source: Jasper et al. 2026 (mass) on IEA PVPS T12-33:2026 (composition); Reg. 548/2014 Tier 2 (losses)

nodes.name: Off-site hydrogen producer
nodes.rating: grey SMR · blue SMR + CCS · turquoise pyrolysis · green PEM (one or two colours)
nodes.model: h2_buy[t] in kg, unbounded (no delivery limit), priced and scored per kg at the gate.
nodes.term: Bought hydrogen — one term per stream, keyed 'bought H2 (<colour>)'; one or two streams
nodes.source: Hermesmann & Müller 2022 (fossil, 30 bar at the plant), Gerloff 2021 (green); h2_prices.py

nodes.name: Compression onto a tube trailer
nodes.rating: to 200 bar: 1.19 kWh/kg (fossil), 1.19 (green)
nodes.model: Charged in both objectives at the seller's electricity; not drawn from the site bus.

nodes.name: Road haulage to site
nodes.rating: distance unknown (seller location)
nodes.model: Not modelled: no fuel, no losses. Arriving hydrogen enters the tank at coefficient 1.

nodes.name: 20 kV site bus — the LP's single node
nodes.rating: every source in, every load out, each half-hour
nodes.model: Σ supply − charging − electrolysis − no-load losses = demand, each half-hour. A copper plate: no internal network, no cable lengths. Curtailment happens here (supply below availability).

nodes.name: Data-centre MV/LV distribution, switchgear, UPS
nodes.rating: inside the facility
nodes.model: Not modelled separately (closed as negligible 4 Sep). The facility's own losses are in its PUE; the UPS battery is in Zhang's facility inventory.

nodes.name: IT load — servers, storage, network
nodes.rating: 100 MW IT (reference run), flat
nodes.model: demand[t] = IT × PUE, flat at 100 % all year.

nodes.name: Cooling and auxiliaries
nodes.rating: (PUE − 1) × IT = 40 MW at PUE 1.4
nodes.model: The PUE share of demand. Default PUE 1.4 (Zhang's own); the page lets the user choose.

nodes.name: Standby diesel genset
nodes.rating: backup only
nodes.model: Excluded from the LP (backup is a decision variable); scored and reported in the facility.

nodes.name: Unserved load
nodes.rating: 0 by default (hard reliability constraint)
nodes.model: unserved[t] ≤ allowance; penalised at VoLL in both objectives (£100,000/MWh; 1,266 t CO₂e/MWh). Not an energy source.

edges.label: 20 kV AC
edges.loss: cable losses inside the net factor

solar.label: Solar
solar.chain: 1 kWh DC at the modules → 0.90 after system losses → about 0.897 at the bus, less no-load

wind.label: Wind
wind.chain: 1 kWh at one turbine's terminals → 0.851 net of the farm → about 0.849 at the bus, less no-load

grid.label: GB grid
grid.chain: 1.0338 kWh generated per kWh at the meter → 0.9993 through the intake, less no-load

battery.label: Battery
battery.chain: 1 kWh charged → 0.88 discharged (0.938 each way); usable 90% of nameplate

hydrogen.label: Hydrogen, made on site
hydrogen.chain: 1 MWh into a PEM electrolyser → 18.5 kg H₂ → 0.293 MWh back from the fuel cell (29.3% round trip; SOEC 35.7% plus heat)

bought.label: Hydrogen, bought
bought.chain: 1 kg delivered → 15.8 kWh at the bus (fuel cell 47.5% net)
